title: Classifying Action Items for Semantic Email
abstract: Presents a rule-based system for recognizing email action items such as task assignments and meeting proposals. Its speech-act model structures action items with an Action, an Object, and where applicable a Subject or agent, and distinguishes actions including Request, Assign, Suggest, and Deliver.

title: *SEM 2012 Shared Task: Resolving the Scope and Focus of Negation
abstract: Defines shared tasks for identifying negation cues, their scope, and focus. Scope-sensitive negation is transferable to preventing negated actions from being incorrectly extracted as live requests, commitments, or decisions.

title: Detecting Emails Containing Requests for Action
abstract: Detects email messages containing requests for action and improves classification by first segmenting messages into functional zones and restricting request detection to relevant content. The evaluated target is primarily message-level presence, so it is most useful as act-detection evidence rather than complete action-slot extraction.

title: Detecting Action Items in Multi-party Meetings: Annotation and Initial Experiments
abstract: Defines action items as social actions involving a task description, timeframe, owner, and participant agreement, and introduces a hierarchical utterance-role annotation scheme for the assignment process. It investigates automatic detection while targeting extraction of information useful for reporting and summarization.
venue: Machine Learning for Multimodal Interaction, MLMI 2006

title: Detecting and Summarizing Action Items in Multi-Party Dialogue
abstract: Detects subdialogues in which action items are proposed, discussed, and committed to, then uses semantic parsing to extract phrases that summarize the tasks involved. This directly supports source-grounded extraction rather than unconstrained action-item generation.
venue: 8th SIGdial Workshop on Discourse and Dialogue

title: Shallow Discourse Structure for Action Item Detection
abstract: Uses shallow discourse structure and a hierarchical annotation scheme to detect action-item assignment regions in meeting transcripts. The work explicitly targets properties including responsible party, task, and deadline rather than treating an action item as an isolated sentence label.
venue: Analyzing Conversations in Text and Speech

title: Extracting Decisions from Multi-Party Dialogue Using Directed Graphical Models and Semantic Similarity
abstract: Uses directed graphical models to detect decision discussions and distinguishes dialogue-act roles such as the issue under discussion and its resolution. It also summarizes decisions by extracting phrases from the source dialogue rather than generating unsupported decisions.

title: Meeting Action Item Detection with Regularized Context Modeling
abstract: Introduces a manually annotated Chinese meeting corpus for action-item detection and a Context-Drop method that exploits local and global conversational context with contrastive learning. Experiments cover the new Chinese corpus and the English AMI corpus.

title: Can Requests-for-Action and Commitments-to-Act be Reliably Identified in Email Messages?
abstract: Reports an exploratory annotation study in which human coders label the presence and strength of Requests-for-Action and Commitments-to-Act in workplace email at sentence level. The study establishes empirical annotation evidence for distinguishing requests that impose action on recipients from promises by senders.

title: Requests and Commitments in Email are More Complex Than You Think: Eight Reasons to be Cautious
abstract: Analyzes difficult real-world cases encountered when annotating and extracting workplace-email requests and commitments, identifying eight categories of problematic phenomena and proposing annotation treatments. It is particularly relevant to conditional, repeated, ambiguous, and context-dependent action evidence.

title: The nature of requests and commitments in email messages
abstract: Develops precise utterance-level definitions for requests and commitments in workplace email using speech-act theory and two annotation experiments on Enron email. It explicitly focuses on utterances that place responsibility for action on the sender or recipients and analyzes difficult surface realizations.

title: Using Speech Acts to Categorize Email and Identify Email Genres
abstract: Defines email-oriented speech acts and uses them to characterize communicative purpose and email genres. The contribution is useful as an email speech-act taxonomy and act-detection baseline rather than as a slot extractor.

title: TimeML: Robust Specification of Event and Temporal Expressions in Text
abstract: Defines a markup language for events, temporal expressions, and temporal links that relate events to times and to other events. The event-time relation layer is directly relevant to linking a deadline expression to the action it constrains rather than extracting dates in isolation.

title: Dialogue act modeling for automatic tagging and recognition of conversational speech
abstract: Develops statistical dialogue-act tagging for conversational speech using lexical, prosodic, and discourse-sequence models. It provides transferable methods for modeling contextual dependencies among speech acts, including agreement and action-oriented dialogue functions.

title: On the collective classification of email "speech acts"
abstract: Classifies email messages for email acts such as requests and commitments and exploits sequential dependencies between messages in the same thread using collective classification. It provides useful evidence for contextual speech-act detection but remains primarily message-level classification.

title: Detecting Action-Items in E-mail
abstract: Detects emails that require action or response and, importantly, highlights the specific text expressing the request. The work explicitly contrasts localized action-item detection with whole-message text categorization.

title: The Possible, the Plausible, and the Desirable: Event-Based Modality Detection for Language Processing
abstract: Models modality as a relation between modal expressions and the events they modify, covering a wider range of modal constructions than cue-only classification. The event-scoped representation is useful for distinguishing the status of an action rather than merely detecting a modal word.
